title: Trump Threatens to Strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain as Nuclear Standoff Escalates
excerpt: The US president said forces would hit the fortified underground facility near Natanz 'pretty soon,' as Israeli intelligence reports Tehran moved centrifuges there after last year's strikes.
body:
President Donald Trump escalated his rhetoric against Iran on Tuesday, declaring that US forces would attack Pickaxe Mountain — a secretive underground nuclear facility near the city of Natanz — "very probably pretty soon."

"We'll be hitting that area very probably pretty soon. And there's not a thing they can do about it," Trump told reporters during a meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office. "Normally, I wouldn't say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that."

What Is Pickaxe Mountain?

Pickaxe Mountain — formally Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La — is a fortified facility about a mile south of Iran's Natanz uranium-enrichment complex, roughly 140 miles south of Tehran. Buried at least 328 feet underground, it houses two tunnel complexes with hardened concrete entrances designed to withstand airstrikes.

Construction began in 2020, when Iran declared the site to the International Atomic Energy Agency as a future centrifuge-assembly facility. Activity intensified after Israel and the US struck three Iranian nuclear facilities — Natanz, Isfahan, and Fordow — during the 12-Day War in June 2025. Neither country struck Pickaxe Mountain at the time.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, citing Israeli intelligence, that Tehran moved thousands of advanced enrichment centrifuges and part of its enriched uranium stockpile to the mountain after those strikes. Iran is believed to hold close to 1,000 pounds of 60% enriched material — near weapons-grade levels — at or near the site.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily."

— Donald Trump, US President

Experts Question Feasibility

Nonproliferation analysts doubt the US can inflict decisive damage on the deeply buried complex. James Acton, who co-leads the Carnegie Endowment's nuclear policy programme, said the US can likely do no more than collapse access tunnels. "That isn't a game changer," Acton posted on X.

The Institute for Science and International Security noted the facility's dependence on ventilation, power, and personnel access presents exploitable vulnerabilities. David Albright, the institute's president, called the Israeli assessment "plausible," citing 15 months of nonstop construction activity around the site.

Iran Warns of Escalation

Tehran responded swiftly. State media reported early Wednesday that any US attack on nuclear facilities would be treated as an expansion of the war. Iran maintains its nuclear programme is solely for peaceful energy purposes.

Trump downplayed the Israeli intelligence. "It doesn't mean anything unless they have the material," he said. "You're talking about the centrifuges. They don't have it. We follow the material."

"And there's not a thing they can do about it," Trump told reporters during a meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office."

The exchange came as the US military conducted an 11th consecutive night of airstrikes, with explosions reported in Tehran, the southeastern port of Chabahar, and Bushehr, home to Iran's only nuclear power plant. Trump confirmed 18 US service members have been killed since the conflict began.

Energy Markets Under Pressure

The nuclear standoff is compounding a broader energy crisis. Brent crude has climbed above $91 a barrel, with US gasoline back over $4 a gallon, after Yemen's Houthis announced a naval blockade targeting Saudi oil shipments. Three tankers carrying Saudi crude bound for China and India reversed course in the Red Sea on Tuesday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Manila on Wednesday that Washington remains "always committed to diplomacy" but questioned Iran's seriousness about negotiations. For India, a major buyer of Gulf crude, any disruption to the Strait of Hormuz or Red Sea shipping lanes will drive up energy costs and inflation at home. The outcome of the Pickaxe Mountain standoff may determine whether the US-Iran conflict remains contained or spirals into a direct confrontation over nuclear weapons.
